analysis.one_liner: Gives people in managed care plans the right to appeal denied care to outside reviewers and sue their health plans.
analysis.headline: The Bipartisan Patient Protection Act of 2001 drew 192 House cosponsors — including 181 of 208 Democrats — but never got a vote in any of the three committees it was sent to, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set national rules for managed care: health plans would have to make coverage decisions quickly, give written reasons for denials, let patients appeal denials to an independent outside reviewer, cover emergency-room visits without pre-approval, and stop restricting what doctors can tell patients. It also would have let patients sue their health plan in court for damages when a denied claim caused harm. To soften the cost, it added tax breaks for self-employed people buying insurance and a credit for small businesses.
analysis.who_benefits: People enrolled in employer health plans and managed care insurance — roughly most working Americans with job-based coverage — who today can be denied care by a plan's reviewers with limited recourse. Patients with serious illnesses who need specialists, emergency care, clinical trials, or expedited decisions gain the most. Doctors gain protections against plan interference and discriminatory exclusion, and self-employed people gain a full tax deduction for their premiums.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People in employer and managed care plans

how_it_helps.text: Plans must run utilization review only through qualified personnel, may not pay reviewers in ways that encourage denials, and must decide prior-authorizations within 14 days — or 72 hours when a doctor certifies the delay would seriously jeopardize a patient's health [S2][S3].

Patients denied care gain the right to an independent external appeal by a medical reviewer with no financial stake in the outcome, and the plan is legally bound to comply — with civil penalties up to $1,000 a day and a $10,000 penalty for ignoring a reviewer's order [S3].
The bill creates a right to sue under ERISA for patients whose plans improperly deny care, ending the shield that let employer-sponsored plans escape most damages claims [S2][S3].

Plans must cover emergency care without prior approval at in-network cost levels, must offer patients a point-of-service option to go outside the network, must cover approved clinical trials and a minimum hospital stay after mastectomy, and may not gag doctors from discussing treatment options with patients [S2][S3].
The self-employed could deduct 100% of health insurance costs and small businesses could claim a credit for providing coverage, and medical savings accounts were expanded [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and managed care plans bear the direct cost: new claims-handling deadlines, independent reviews they must pay for, penalties, and exposure to lawsuits from denied-care cases, which they warn would raise premiums. Employers who self-fund plans could face liability as plan sponsors. Some of the added cost would flow back to working families as higher premiums.

drawbacks.text: Critics argued the new right to sue would drive up litigation and health premiums, spreading costs to workers and employers who pay for coverage — a cost an honest supporter had to concede [S2].
The compliance burden on plans — strict decision timelines, mandatory outside reviews, and penalties for missed deadlines — added administrative costs that could be passed through in premiums [S3].

The tax provisions expanded medical savings accounts and added deductions and credits that primarily benefit taxpayers who itemize or can front premium costs, rather than the lowest-income uninsured [S2][S3].
The point-of-service choice option lets enrollees go outside the network only by bearing the extra cost themselves, so patient choice depends on ability to pay [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients facing denied or delayed care, the protections were substantial and directly enforceable. The honest counterweight is real: liability and compliance costs would likely raise premiums somewhat, and the bill's tax sweeteners skew toward those who can afford coverage already. On balance the bill's central effect — outside review and court recourse for denied care — falls on insurers and plan sponsors, not on patients' wallets, though not all of the cost stops there.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees and then to their health subcommittees, where it sat; the sponsor gave three rounds of floor remarks promoting it, but no committee ever voted to send it to the floor and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Greg Ganske (R-IA) and John Dingell (D-MI) introduced the bill on February 8, 2001, with an unusually broad bipartisan cosponsor list printed in the bill itself [S1][S3].
It was referred to three committees — Energy and Commerce, Education and the Workforce, and Ways and Means — and within weeks to the Health and Employer-Employee Relations subcommittees [S5].
The bill accumulated 192 cosponsors: 181 of 208 House Democrats, 10 of 223 House Republicans, and the chamber's sole Independent [S4].

The last action of any kind was the sponsor's third set of introductory remarks on June 28, 2001; no committee or subcommittee took up the bill again before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and managed care plans are better off: no outside-appeal mandate, no new penalties, and no right to sue under ERISA ever took effect, and employers sponsoring self-funded plans kept their litigation shield. Patients denied care by their plans gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and managed care plans

for.name: John Dingell

for.what_they_did: Co-led introduction of the bill, lending it bipartisan weight

sides.party_line_note: Support was strongly bipartisan on paper — 181 of 208 Democrats and 10 of 223 Republicans cosponsored — but the bill's failure came from the House Republican leadership and committees, which never moved it, while a narrower rival bill was advanced instead.

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care plans
industries.note: The bill imposes binding outside review of denied claims, strict decision deadlines, penalties of up to $1,000 a day for ignoring reviewers, and a right to sue — costs the plans had fought for years. Its cost to insurers is precisely the protection it gives patients.
By adding civil remedies under ERISA, the bill would have ended the near-total litigation shield these plans enjoyed, exposing plan sponsors to damages suits over denied care.

The bill bars plans from gagging doctor-patient communications, discriminating against licensed professionals, or paying bonuses that reward claim denials — protections for clinical judgment that line up with patient interests.
Expanded Archer MSAs and new tax deductions would widen tax-advantaged insurance products, a benefit weighted toward higher-income taxpayers.
